1.q: מִ֥י הֶאֱמִ֖ין לִ⁠שְׁמֻעָתֵ֑⁠נוּ וּ⁠זְר֥וֹעַ יְהוָ֖ה עַל מִ֥י נִגְלָֽתָה
1.note: Isaiah is using the question form to express that hardly anyone will believe the message about the servant or recognize the power of Yahweh at work in him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Hardly anyone will believe our report, and to hardly anyone will the arm of Yahweh be revealed!]

Here, **the arm of Yahweh** represents “the power of Yahweh.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and to whom will the power of Yahweh be revealed]

The expression **be revealed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [will Yahweh reveal his arm]

2.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a shoot** or **a root** growing up in dry ground is fragile and easily overlooked, so the servant was humble and unremarkable as he grew up. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as fragile and unremarkable as a shoot or a root growing up in dry ground]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he grew up like a root from dry ground]

3.note: The expression **was despised** is a passive verbal form. While the term **rejected** is an adjective in Hebrew, to speakers of many languages, it may seem like a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use these forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Men despised and rejected him]

Isaiah is using **a man of sorrows and acquainted of grief** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a person who has experienced much suffering.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a person who has experienced much suffering]

Hiding one’s face from someone, that is, not looking at that person, was a symbolic action in this culture by which someone showed disregard for a person. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. The UST models one way to do that.

4.note: Here Isaiah is speaking as if **our griefs** and **our sorrows** were a heavy responsibility that the servant **bore** and **carried**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he took our griefs upon himself, and he took our sorrows upon himself]

Isaiah is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he bore** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize who it was who bore our griefs. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [it was he, the man I am describing, who bore]

Isaiah is stating the pronoun **we** separately, even though the verb translated as **we esteemed** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that the role of the people of Israel. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But we, the people of Israel, esteemed him]

The words **stricken**, **struck of God**, and **afflicted** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [as one whom God was striking, whom God was hitting, and whom God was afflicting]

5.q: וְ⁠הוּא֙ מְחֹלָ֣ל מִ⁠פְּשָׁעֵ֔⁠נוּ מְדֻכָּ֖א מֵ⁠עֲוֺנֹתֵ֑י⁠נוּ מוּסַ֤ר שְׁלוֹמֵ֨⁠נוּ֙ עָלָ֔י⁠ו וּ⁠בַ⁠חֲבֻרָת֖⁠וֹ נִרְפָּא לָֽ⁠נוּ
5.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [But he was severely wounded because of all our sins. The discipline of our peace was on him, and by his wounds it is healed for us]

The expression **was pierced** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But he endured piercing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgressions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the wrong things we did]

The expression **crushed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God crushed him]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because we acted wickedly]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **discipline** that brings about our **peace**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The discipline that brings us peace]

Here Isaiah is speaking of the restoration that the servant brings about as if it were physical healing that comes by his **wounds**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and because of his wounds, we are restored]

The expression **is healed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God heals us]

6.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **sheep** wander away from their shepherd and become lost, so all of us have strayed from God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [All of us have wandered away from God, just as sheep stray from their shepherd]

Here Isaiah is speaking of each person’s conduct as if it were a **way** or road that the person walks along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each of us has turned to his own manner of living]

Isaiah is not referring to a specific **man**. He means each person, people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [each person to their own way]

6.q: וַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ הִפְגִּ֣יעַ בּ֔⁠וֹ אֵ֖ת עֲוֺ֥ן כֻּלָּֽ⁠נוּ
6.note: Here Isaiah is speaking as if the **iniquity** of everyone were a heavy load that Yahweh caused to **land on** the servant. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh has caused him to suffer the punishment for the iniquity of all of us]

7.note: The words **oppressed** and **afflicted** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Others oppressed him, and they afflicted him]

Isaiah is using **he did not open his mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he remained silent and did not protest.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he stayed silent]

The expression **was led** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Others led him]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a lamb** does not resist when it is led away to be killed, so the servant did not resist when people led him away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [without resisting, like a lamb that does not resist being led to be slaughtered]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a ewe** stays silent while it is being sheared, so the servant remained silent and did not protest. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and just as a ewe does not protest but stays silent while its shearers cut its wool]

8.note: The phrase **coercion** and **judgment** expresses a single idea. The word **coercion** tells more about this **judgment**, indicating that it was an oppressive and unjust judgment. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [By an oppressive judgment] or [By an unjust trial]

The expression **was taken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they took him away]

Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that no one at the time gave any thought to the injustice of what happened to the servant. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one considered his generation.]

Here Isaiah is speaking of the servant’s death as if he were **cut off** from **the land of the living**, that is, removed from among those who are alive. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he was killed and no longer among the living]

The expression **was cut off** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people cut him off]

Some ancient manuscripts read “my people.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “his people.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **affliction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he was afflicted]

9.note: The pronoun **one** refers to people in general, not to a specific individual. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And people would have made]

Isaiah is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the wicked people]

Some ancient manuscripts read “deaths.” The ULT follows that reading. An important ancient manuscripts reads “death.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

If **deaths** is the original reading, Isaiah is using a plural form where he could have used the singular form. This suggests that he is using the plural form to emphasize the significance of the servant’s death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [in his momentous death]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent deeds]

Here, **his mouth** represents “his speech.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and there was no deceit in his speech]

10.note: The marking of the verb that the ULT translates as **you make** also allows it to be translated as **his soul makes**. If that is correct, then Isaiah is using one part of the servant, his **soul**, to mean all of him in making a **guilt offering**, specifically of his own life on behalf of others. Alternate translation: [When his soul makes a guilt offering] or [When he offers his life as a guilt offering]

Here Isaiah shifts to addressing Yahweh directly in the second person with the word **you**, even though he refers to Yahweh in the third person as **Yahweh** elsewhere in this verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could continue to refer to Yahweh in the third person here. Alternate translation: [he makes his soul a guilt offering]

Here Isaiah is speaking of the servant’s life as if it were a **guilt offering**, a sacrifice presented to Yahweh to remove people’s guilt. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you offer his life to remove people’s guilt]

Here Isaiah is speaking of the servant’s descendants as if they were **seed** that grows from a plant. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will see his descendants]

Isaiah is using **he will lengthen days** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will live a long time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will live a long time]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pleasure**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what pleases Yahweh]

Here, **his hand** represents “the servant’s power to accomplish things.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [through his power]

11.note: Some ancient manuscripts read “he will see”. The ULT follows that reading. An important ancient manuscript reads “he will see light”. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **knowledge**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [By what he knows]

Here Yahweh begins to speak directly, but the text does not mark the start of his words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that this is the beginning of a direct quotation from Yahweh.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the **iniquities** of many people were a heavy burden that the servant would **bear**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he, he will suffer the punishment for their sins]

12.note: Yahweh is using the adjective **great** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [among the great people]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the reward he will give the servant as if the servant were a victorious warrior who **will divide the spoil** with other soldiers after a battle. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will give him a rich reward along with the powerful]

Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh’s servant sacrificing his life as if it had been a liquid that he **poured out** of a container. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he freely gave up his life]

Yahweh is using **he was numbered with transgressors** as a common expression of the culture to mean “people counted him as a criminal.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and people counted him as a criminal] or [and people considered him to be a criminal]

The expression **was numbered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people counted him] or [people considered him]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the **sin** of many people were a heavy burden that the servant **bore**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he received the punishment for the sins of many people] or [he suffered the punishment for the sins of many people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sin**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what many people had sinned]
